analysis.one_liner: Lets citizens sue state officials for violating their constitutional rights, eliminating the qualified immunity defense.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote in the House Judiciary Committee, where it sat after introduction in June 2020 until the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would change the nation's main civil rights lawsuit law, written in 1871, so that people who say a government employee violated their constitutional rights can actually win money damages in court. It would eliminate the defense known as qualified immunity, which courts have used to shield officials unless a prior case with nearly identical facts exists. It would also make state and local governments financially responsible for their employees' violations and require them to pay any judgment against the employee, and it would let federal prosecutors sue on a victim's behalf.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by government officials acting in their official capacity — most commonly victims of police or other government misconduct, and their families. They would no longer lose cases merely because no earlier court decision covered the exact same facts, and they would gain a fallback in which a U.S. Attorney could sue for them.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the qualified immunity defense: a defendant sued for an official act could no longer argue the act did not violate a 'clearly established' right, the defense courts created in cases like Harlow v. Fitzgerald that the bill's findings say nullifies the remedy unless a nearly identical prior case exists [S2][S3].

Makes the state or territory that employs the official vicariously liable when the violation is attributable to Fourteenth Amendment violations by the state, so victims could collect from the government rather than only from an individual [S2][S3].

Requires states to indemnify employees found liable for official acts, and authorizes any U.S. Attorney to bring a civil action on behalf of a victim, giving people without their own lawyer a path to court [S2][S3].
The changes would apply to cases already pending as well as future cases [S3].

analysis.who_pays: State, territorial, and District of Columbia governments — ultimately their taxpayers — would pay damages and indemnification for employees' constitutional violations. Individual officials would lose their personal shield from liability for official acts, though the bill requires the government to pay judgments against them.
analysis.who_pays_short: State and local governments and taxpayers

drawbacks.text: State and local governments would face new, potentially large financial liability for employees' violations, with the bill explicitly applying to cases already pending at enactment, which could produce a wave of new claims [S3].

Eliminating the qualified immunity defense could expose officials to personal suits for ordinary on-the-job judgment calls, the concern supporters of the current doctrine raise; the bill's indemnification provision shifts the money to government but not the burden of litigation [S3].

The vicarious liability and indemnification provisions only apply when the violation is 'attributable to violations of the 14th Amendment by the State' — a narrower trigger than a general employer-liability rule, leaving the bill's coverage less sweeping than its stated purpose [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people whose constitutional rights are violated, the bill restores a remedy that courts have largely closed off, which is a real and significant gain. The cost is borne by taxpayers through government liability and indemnification, and the bill applies retroactively to pending cases, which would concentrate new costs on state budgets in the short run. The narrow Fourteenth Amendment trigger for government liability makes the design less comprehensive than the problem it describes.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2020, referred to the House Judiciary Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Marc Veasey introduced the bill on June 4, 2020, during the wave of police-accountability legislation following George Floyd's death, and it was referred to the House Judiciary Committee the same day [S1][S5].
It drew a single cosponsor, one House Democrat [S4].
No further action appears in its history: the House Judiciary Committee never reported the bill and the House never voted on it before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government entities and officials who would have faced liability under the bill are better off, since the qualified immunity defense and the limits on suing governments remain intact; victims of constitutional violations gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Marc A. Veasey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee on June 4, 2020.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral (chair: Rep. Jerrold Nadler, D-NY)
against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or report for the remainder of the 116th Congress, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its one cosponsor were both Democrats, and no Republican supported the bill; broader 2020 efforts to end qualified immunity stalled largely along party lines after Democrats passed the George Floyd Justice in Policing Act and Senate Republicans declined to include the reform.

industries.note: The bill would make governments financially responsible for employees' constitutional violations and require them to pay judgments and indemnify officials, ending the current arrangement in which courts have held governments not liable for damages caused by their employees under cases like Monell. Governments' interest in avoiding lawsuits runs directly against victims' interest in compensation.

industries.industry: Government liability insurers and legal-defense interests
industries.note: More claims against governments, with the qualified immunity defense removed, would increase payouts and defense costs for the insurers and law firms that currently defend officials and settle civil rights cases cheaply.
